    Content from Introduction to Quarto Dashboards

    Last updated on 2026-11-18 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Why are dashboards a useful way to present OA monitoring data?
    • What is Quarto, and how is a Quarto document structured?
    • What are the main components of a Quarto dashboard?

    Objectives

    • Explain why dashboards are useful for OA monitoring
    • Describe what Quarto is and name the main components of a Quarto document
    • Describe what a Quarto dashboard is and how it relates to other Quarto output formats
    • Describe the main building blocks of a Quarto dashboard

    Why dashboards for OA monitoring?

    A dashboard presents the most important information about a topic on a single screen, so it can be understood at a glance, rather than requiring someone to read through a long report. In the context of Open Access (OA) this is useful for:

    • Monitoring: keeping an eye on numbers that change over time, for example how many of your institution’s publications are Open Access this year compared to last year, or how article processing charge (APC) spending develops across publishers
    • Communicating with non-technical audiences: a library director, university management or a funding body wants the headline numbers (“our OA share is now 62%”) instead of the analysis code or a lengthy statistical report
    • Supporting negotiations and decisions: libraries can use dashboards to track transformative agreements with publishers (how much is spent vs. how many articles are published open access under that deal), which directly informs whether an agreement is worth renewing
    • Staying up to date automatically: because a Quarto dashboard is generated from code, re-running it against new data (for example an updated export from your repository or a bibliometric database) produces an updated dashboard, without rebuilding it by hand

    What is Quarto?

    Quarto is an open-source, multi-language publishing system. It combines plain text written in Markdown with code (in R, or other languages like Python or Julia) to produce a finished document. Quarto documents can be written in several editors, such as RStudio, JupyterLab, and Visual Studio Code, so Quarto isn’t tied to R and RStudio specifically.

    With Quarto the same underlying document can be rendered into many output formats: HTML pages, PDFs, Word documents, presentations, websites, books and, as we will see, dashboards. Which one you get depends on the format you choose; everything else about how you write the document stays more or less the same.

    This lesson only covers what you need to build a dashboard. Quarto itself is much bigger. If you would like a fuller introduction, two good starting points are the official Quarto Get Started guide and the Carpentries Incubator lesson Reproducible Publications with Quarto.

    The anatomy of a Quarto document

    A Quarto document is a plain-text file with the extension .qmd. It consists of three main components:

    MARKDOWN 

    ---
title: "My first document"
format: html
---

## A heading

Some text with **bold** words.

``` r
1 + 1
```
    1. A YAML header at the very top, between two lines of three dashes (---). It holds settings for the whole document, such as the title and the output format.
    2. Markdown text, which gives the document its structure (headings, lists, links, images). We practise Markdown syntax in the next episode.
    3. Code chunks, which run code and put the result (a number, a table, a chart) into the document. We meet them in a later episode.

    When you render the file, Quarto runs the code, combines the results with the text and writes the output file, for example a .html file. Change the data or the code, render again, and you get an updated document.

    Callout

    What is YAML?

    YAML (“YAML Ain’t Markup Language”) is a human-readable format for writing settings as key: value pairs. It is not specific to Quarto; many tools use it for configuration files.

    • Each setting is written as key: value
    • Indentation (using spaces, not tabs) shows that one setting belongs inside another
    • In a Quarto document, the YAML block is marked off by three dashes (---) at the start and end

    What is a Quarto dashboard?

    A Quarto dashboard is one of several predefined output formats built into Quarto. Under the hood, a dashboard is essentially a regular HTML page with a predefined layout: instead of flowing top to bottom like a report, your content is arranged into a grid of rows, columns and cards. Setting the format option in the YAML header to dashboard is all it takes:

    YAML 

    ---
title: "My OA Dashboard"
format: dashboard
---

    Components of a Quarto dashboard

    Let us go through the components we will build in this lesson:

    Navigation bar: the bar at the top of every dashboard. It shows the title (and, later, a logo) and, if you have more than one page, a tab for each page.

    Pages: each page is shown as its own tab in the navigation bar. A single-page dashboard shows no page tabs.

    Rows and columns: a page is divided into rows (the default) or columns. Rows can be split further into columns, and columns into rows. In the figure, the two teal cards sit side by side as columns within one row, and the grey card below forms a second row on its own. You can switch the default with the orientation setting in the YAML header:

    YAML 

    format:
  dashboard:
    orientation: columns

    Note how orientation is indented one level further than dashboard, and dashboard one level further than format. That indentation nests orientation inside dashboard, which is itself nested inside format.

    Cards: the bordered panels that hold your content. The output of every code chunk becomes a card automatically; you do not have to create them explicitly. Text and images can be put into cards too.

    Value boxes: a special kind of card for prominently displaying a single number, such as “OA share: 62%”.

    Two further components exist that we will not build in this lesson, but you will meet them in the Quarto documentation: sidebars (a panel at the side, often used for input controls like dropdown menues or sliders) and tabsets (tabs that stack two cards together).

    Callout

    How are these components created?

    In a Quarto dashboard, Markdown headings define the layout:

    • a level 1 heading (#) starts a new page
    • a level 2 heading (##) starts a new row or column

    and code chunks produce the content of the cards. We learn the syntax in the next episodes and use it when we build the dashboard.

    Key Points

    • Dashboards present key information at a glance, which is useful for OA monitoring, communicating with non-technical audiences, and staying up to date automatically
    • A Quarto document has three main components: a YAML header, Markdown text and code chunks
    • Setting format: dashboard in the YAML header renders the document as a dashboard
    • A dashboard consists of a navigation bar, pages, rows, columns and cards; value boxes are special cards for a single number
    • Markdown headings define the layout, code chunks produce the content

    Content from Introduction to Markdown

    Last updated on 2026-11-18 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What is Markdown, and why do we need it for Quarto dashboards?
    • How do you create headings, bold text, lists, links and images in Markdown?
    • How do you tell Quarto to show code and to run code?

    Objectives

    • Explain what Markdown is and why Quarto documents use it
    • Write headings of different levels and explain why heading levels matter for dashboards
    • Format text in bold and italics and create bulleted and numbered lists
    • Create links and add images with alt text
    • Distinguish between inline code, a highlighted code block and an executable code chunk
    Callout

    You might skip this episode if…

    You already write Markdown (headings, lists, links, images, code blocks) and know the difference between a code block and an executable code chunk.

    What is Markdown?

    Markdown is a lightweight way of formatting text using plain-text symbols. Instead of clicking a “bold” button in a word processor, you type symbols like ** around your text. A program then turns these symbols into formatted output, for example HTML, PDF or, in our case, a Quarto dashboard.

    Quarto uses a version of Markdown called Pandoc-flavored Markdown. Markdown matters for this lesson in particular, because Quarto dashboards use headings to define the layout:

    • A level 1 heading (#) starts a new dashboard page
    • A level 2 heading (##) starts a new dashboard row or column

    We will use this in a later episode. For now, we practise the syntax.

    Headings

    Headings are created with one or more hash symbols (#) at the start of a line, followed by a space and the heading text. The more hash symbols, the lower the heading level and the smaller the font size.

    MARKDOWN 

    # Heading level 1
## Heading level 2
### Heading level 3
#### Heading level 4
    Callout

    Two things to watch out for

    • Missing space: #Heading does not work, # Heading does.
    • Missing empty line: put an empty line before every heading (and before every list). Otherwise it may be treated as regular text, and in a dashboard your layout might not work as expected.
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Headings

    You are writing a short guide on Open Access for your institution. The indentation below shows which level each heading belongs to:

    Open Access at Our University
    Publishing routes
        Gold Open Access
        Green Open Access
    OA Funding
        Article processing charges

    Write this structure as Markdown headings, using the correct heading levels.

    Start with the line that has no indentation. It is the main title, so it gets level 1.

    MARKDOWN 

    # Open Access at Our University

## Publishing routes

### Gold Open Access

### Green Open Access

## OA Funding

### Article processing charges

    The further a line is indented, the more hash symbols it gets. Later in this lesson you will use exactly this idea to decide what becomes a page, a row or a column in your dashboard.

    Emphasis and lists

    Surround text with one asterisk to make it italic and with two to make it bold:

    MARKDOWN 

    *This text is italic*

**This text is bold**

    Bulleted lists start with a dash and a space (-) before each item, numbered lists with a number, a period and a space (1.). Remember the empty line before a list:

    MARKDOWN 

    - open access
- open data
- open source

1. Collect your data
2. Clean your data
3. Build your dashboard

    This renders as:

    • open access
    • open data
    • open source
    1. Collect your data
    2. Clean your data
    3. Build your dashboard

    Links and images

    To create a link, put the link text in square brackets, directly followed by the URL in round brackets:

    MARKDOWN 

    [Unpaywall](https://unpaywall.org)

    This renders as: Unpaywall. If you want to show the URL itself, wrap it in angle brackets: <https://openalex.org>.

    Adding an image works almost like a link, but with an exclamation mark ! in front. The text in the square brackets becomes the alt text: a short description that screen readers read out and that is shown if the image cannot be loaded. Alt text makes images accessible to more people.

    MARKDOWN 

    ![The Open Access logo, an open padlock](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg)

    This renders as an image of the Open Access logo:

    You will use exactly this image syntax again when you build the dashboard.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Links and images

    You are preparing the “Useful resources” section of an OA guide.

    1. Turn this URL into a Markdown link with the link text “Directory of Open Access Journals”: https://doaj.org
    2. Add a Markdown image using the URL below, and write a short, meaningful alt text for it: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/DOAJ_logo.png

    MARKDOWN 

    [Directory of Open Access Journals](https://doaj.org)

![Logo of the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ)](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/DOAJ_logo.png)

    Any short description of what the image shows works as alt text. “Image” or “logo” alone would not tell a screen reader user much.

    Code: inline, blocks and chunks

    Markdown can mark text as code, which is displayed in a fixed-width (monospace) font. This matters for Quarto, because the content of a dashboard is produced by code.

    Inline code uses single backticks:

    MARKDOWN 

    Use `filter(oa_status == "gold")` to keep only gold Open Access articles.

    A fenced code block uses three backticks on their own line before and after the code. If you add the language name after the opening backticks, the code is coloured and easier to read. It is still only displayed, not run. If you put the language name in curly braces, Quarto treats the block as an executable code chunk: it runs the code and shows the result.

    MARKDOWN 

    ```
summary(articles)
```

```r
summary(articles)
```

```{r}
summary(articles)
```

    Quarto therefore knows three ways to handle code:

    • ```: a plain code block (monospace text)
    • ```r: a highlighted code block (coloured, but not run)
    • ```{r}: an executable code chunk (Quarto runs it and shows the output)

    In a Quarto dashboard, headings define the layout and executable code chunks produce its content. These are the two Markdown building blocks you will use most.

    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Spot the syntax

    Look at the following snippet from an OA guide. Identify (a) the heading level, (b) the bold text, (c) the inline code and (d) the link.

    MARKDOWN 

    ## Gold Open Access

Use the `oa_status` column to find gold articles. You can check journals in
the [DOAJ](https://doaj.org). **Note:** gold Open Access often requires an
article processing charge.

    1. ## Gold Open Access: a level 2 heading

    2. **Note:**: bold text

    3. `oa_status`: inline code

    4. [DOAJ](https://doaj.org): a link

    Callout

    Further reading

    The Quarto documentation has a page on Markdown basics with more syntax than we covered here.

    Key Points

    • Markdown is a lightweight plain-text syntax for formatting text; Quarto is built on it
    • Headings and lists need a space after the symbol and an empty line before them; heading levels (#, ##) will define pages, rows and columns in a dashboard
    • Links use [text](url) and images use ![alt text](url)
    • ```r displays highlighted code, ```{r} runs it

    Content from Introduction to R and RStudio

    Last updated on 2026-11-18 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What are R and RStudio, and why does this lesson use them to build dashboard content?
    • How do you create and work with values in R, using objects, functions, vectors and data frames?
    • How do you install and load an R package?
    • How can you use the pipe operator to chain dplyr verbs together for readable data wrangling?

    Objectives

    • Navigate the RStudio interface, create a project and run code
    • Create objects and vectors, call functions, and build and access columns of a data frame
    • Install packages with install.packages() and load them with library()
    • Use the pipe operator |> together with filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange() and group_by() + summarise() to wrangle a data frame
    Callout

    You might skip this episode if…

    You already know how to work with R/RStudio: creating objects, calling functions, using vectors and data frames, installing and loading packages, chaining steps with the pipe operator (|>) and using basic dplyr verbs (filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange(), group_by() + summarise()). Everything here is general-purpose R, not specific to Quarto dashboards.

    If you skip this episode, please make sure that the packages tidyverse and DT are installed (see Installing packages) and that you have created an RStudio project.

    Callout

    A note before we start

    This episode teaches only the minimum R needed to read and adapt the dashboard code in this lesson. If you want to learn R more thoroughly, Library Carpentry has a dedicated lesson: Introduction to R.

    Why R for dashboards?

    In the Markdown episode, we learned that a fenced code block becomes executable in Quarto when you wrap the language name in curly braces: ```{r} instead of ```r. Every chart, table and value in your dashboard can be the output of an R chunk like that. This episode teaches just enough R for you to read, understand and adapt those chunks.

    R is free, widely used for data analysis in research and libraries, and it has excellent tools for exactly what an OA dashboard needs: reading data, calculating shares and counts, drawing charts and building tables.

    RStudio

    We write and run all our R code in RStudio, a free application (an integrated development environment, IDE) built for working with R. RStudio also works well with Quarto. When you open RStudio, you typically see four panes:

    • Source / Script (top left): where you edit files
    • Console (bottom left): where code actually runs, one command at a time
    • Environment / History (top right): lists the objects you have created, so you can see what currently exists
    • Files / Plots / Packages / Help (bottom right): browse files, view plots, manage packages and read documentation

    Create a new R project

    An RStudio project keeps all files of one project (code, data, images) together in one folder. We create one for our dashboard:

    1. Go to File > New Project...
    2. Choose New Directory, then New Project
    3. Name your project (for example oa-dashboard) and pick a location to save it
    4. Click Create Project

    Create a new Quarto document

    1. Go to File > New File > Quarto Document...
    2. Give it a title, leave the format on the default (HTML) and click Create
    3. Go to File > Save As... (or press Ctrl+S / Cmd+S)
    4. Name the file (e.g. oa-dashboard.qmd) and make sure it is saved in your project folder (the folder of your RStudio project). Click Save

    The saved file should now appear in the Files pane at the bottom right.

    RStudio fills the new document with some example Markdown text and two ```{r} code chunks. We use this document to try things out in this episode, and we turn it into a dashboard later. You can work with it like this:

    • Run a chunk: click the green “play” arrow in the top-right corner of the chunk
    • Insert an empty chunk: press Ctrl+Alt+I (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Option+I (Mac), or use the green Insert button in the toolbar
    • Run a single line: place the cursor on the line and press Ctrl+Enter (Windows/Linux) or Cmd+Enter (Mac)
    • Render the whole document: click the Render button

    The code in the rest of this episode can be typed into a chunk of this document or directly into the Console.

    Objects

    In R, you store a value by giving it a name with the assignment operator <-. Once an object exists, you can reuse it by typing its name.

    R 

    number_of_articles <- 5
number_of_articles

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 5

    You can overwrite an object at any time by assigning a new value to the same name:

    R 

    number_of_articles <- 8
number_of_articles

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 8

    Functions

    A function takes some input (its arguments), does something with it, and returns a result. You call a function by writing its name followed by round brackets containing the arguments.

    R 

    round(3.14159, 2)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 3.14

    Here, round() is the function, 3.14159 is the value to round, and 2 tells it how many decimal places to keep. Functions can also take more than one value at once:

    R 

    sum(4, 8, 15)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 27
    Challenge

    Challenge 1: Objects and functions

    Your institution published 1,382 articles last year, 847 of them open access. Create two objects, all_articles and oa_articles, and use them to calculate the OA share in percent, rounded to one decimal place.

    The share in percent is oa_articles / all_articles * 100. Wrap the calculation in round().

    R 

    all_articles <- 1382
oa_articles <- 847
round(oa_articles / all_articles * 100, 1)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 61.3

    Vectors

    A vector holds several values of the same data type in a single object. You create one with the c() function (“combine”):

    R 

    oa_status <- c("gold", "green", "closed")
oa_status

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "gold"   "green"  "closed"

    You can pick out a single element using square brackets and its position:

    R 

    oa_status[2]

    OUTPUT 

    [1] "green"

    Named vectors

    A vector can also have a name attached to each value:

    R 

    apcs <- c(gold = 2000, hybrid = 2500, diamond = 0)
apcs

    OUTPUT 

       gold  hybrid diamond
   2000    2500       0

    You can now pick out a value by its name instead of its position:

    R 

    apcs["hybrid"]

    OUTPUT 

    hybrid
  2500
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Named vectors

    For the charts in your dashboard you want one colour per OA status. Create a named vector called oa_colors that assigns a colour to three OA statuses: gold should map to "gold", green to "forestgreen" and closed to "grey". Then retrieve the colour for green.

    We will use this vector again when we style the dashboard.

    R 

    oa_colors <- c(gold = "gold", green = "forestgreen", closed = "grey")
oa_colors["green"]

    OUTPUT 

            green
"forestgreen"

    Data frames

    A data frame stores data in rows and columns. Think of it as a small spreadsheet inside R. You can build one with data.frame(). Here is a tiny example of six articles with their OA status and number of citations:

    R 

    articles <- data.frame(
  title = c("Paper A", "Paper B", "Paper C", "Paper D", "Paper E", "Paper F"),
  oa_status = c("gold", "green", "closed", "gold", "closed", "green"),
  citations = c(12, 5, 20, 8, 3, 9)
)
articles

    OUTPUT 

        title oa_status citations
1 Paper A      gold        12
2 Paper B     green         5
3 Paper C    closed        20
4 Paper D      gold         8
5 Paper E    closed         3
6 Paper F     green         9

    To access a single column, use the dollar sign $ between the data frame’s name and the column’s name:

    R 

    articles$citations

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 12  5 20  8  3  9

    Because articles$citations is a vector, you can pass it straight into a function:

    R 

    mean(articles$citations)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 9.5
    Challenge

    Challenge 3: Data frames

    Using the articles data frame, find the highest and the lowest number of citations among the six articles. (Hint: besides sum() and mean(), R has the functions max() and min().)

    R 

    max(articles$citations)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 20

    R 

    min(articles$citations)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 3

    Packages

    Not all functions come built into R. Packages are collections of extra functions that other people have written. Using a package takes two steps:

    1. Install it once on your computer, with install.packages()
    2. Load it with library() at the start of every R session in which you want to use it

    Think of it like a book: you buy it once (install), but you take it off the shelf every time you want to read it (load).

    Installing packages

    Type the install.packages() function directly into the Console, not into a document, because R would otherwise reinstall the packages every time you run or render the document:

    R 

    install.packages("tidyverse")

    For our OA dashboard we need two packages:

    Package What we use it for
    tidyverse wrangling data (dplyr), reading CSV files (readr) and drawing charts (ggplot2)
    DT interactive, searchable tables

    You can install both (or more) in one go by combining the names with c():

    R 

    install.packages(c("tidyverse", "DT"))

    Run this line in the Console now. The installation can take a few minutes and prints a lot of text while it works; that is normal. Wait until the > prompt appears again in the Console.

    Loading packages

    Loading happens inside the document itself, because clicking Render always starts a brand new R session. That is why this line belongs in a chunk:

    R 

    library(tidyverse)

    OUTPUT 

    ── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.4     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

    R 

    library(DT)

    ERROR 

    Error in `library()`:
! there is no package called 'DT'

    Nothing visible happens when a package loads successfully (aside from some startup messages), but afterwards extra functions are available that were not there before, like the dplyr verbs we will use in the next sections. We load DT already now, even though we only use it in a later episode. If both lines run without an error, you know that both packages are available when needed. If R reports there is no package called ‘DT’ (or another name), that package is not installed yet. Install it with install.packages("DT") and try again.

    Callout

    What is the tidyverse?

    tidyverse is not a single package. It is a collection of several packages designed to work well together, including dplyr (for wrangling data), ggplot2 (for plotting) and readr (for reading data files like CSVs). Loading tidyverse loads all of them at once.

    The pipe operator

    The pipe operator |> takes whatever is on its left and feeds it into the function on its right as the first argument. This lets you chain several steps together, left to right, instead of nesting functions inside each other. It is built into R itself (since R 4.1), so you do not need to load any package to use it.

    R 

    articles$citations |> mean() |> round(1)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 9.5

    This does exactly the same thing as round(mean(articles$citations), 1), but it reads left to right, in the order the steps actually happen. When you chain several steps, start a new line after each pipe to keep the code readable:

    R 

    articles$citations |>
  mean() |>
  round(1)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 9.5
    Callout

    A note on %>%

    You may come across a different-looking pipe, %>%, in other R code or tutorials. It comes from the magrittr package and was the original pipe, before R got its own built-in version. It works almost the same way. This lesson uses |> throughout, because it needs no additional package. If you see %>% in someone else’s code, read it the same way: “take what is on the left, and pass it into what is on the right.”

    Challenge

    Challenge 4: Using the pipe

    Rewrite round(sum(articles$citations), 0) using the pipe operator |> instead of nesting the two functions.

    R 

    articles$citations |> 
  sum() |> 
  round(0)

    OUTPUT 

    [1] 57

    A few essential dplyr verbs

    dplyr (loaded as part of the tidyverse) provides a small set of functions, often called “verbs”, for working with data frames. Combined with the pipe, they read almost like plain English. We keep using the articles data frame from before.

    filter() keeps only the rows that match a condition:

    R 

    articles |>
  filter(oa_status == "gold")

    OUTPUT 

        title oa_status citations
1 Paper A      gold        12
2 Paper D      gold         8

    select() keeps only the columns you name:

    R 

    articles |>
  select(title, citations)

    OUTPUT 

        title citations
1 Paper A        12
2 Paper B         5
3 Paper C        20
4 Paper D         8
5 Paper E         3
6 Paper F         9

    mutate() adds a new column (or changes an existing one):

    R 

    articles |>
  mutate(is_oa = oa_status != "closed")

    OUTPUT 

        title oa_status citations is_oa
1 Paper A      gold        12  TRUE
2 Paper B     green         5  TRUE
3 Paper C    closed        20 FALSE
4 Paper D      gold         8  TRUE
5 Paper E    closed         3 FALSE
6 Paper F     green         9  TRUE
    Callout

    = vs. == vs. !=

    These look similar but mean different things:

    • A single = inside a function call names an argument, e.g. mutate(is_oa = ...) creates a column called is_oa.
    • A double == checks whether two values are equal, e.g. oa_status == "gold" asks “is oa_status equal to "gold"?” and returns TRUE or FALSE.
    • != means not equal: oa_status != "closed" is TRUE for every article that is not closed, in other words every open access article.

    Writing = where you meant == is one of the most common early mistakes in R.

    arrange() sorts the rows by the values of a column in ascending order (wrap the column in desc() for descending order):

    R 

    articles |>
  arrange(citations)

    OUTPUT 

        title oa_status citations
1 Paper E    closed         3
2 Paper B     green         5
3 Paper D      gold         8
4 Paper F     green         9
5 Paper A      gold        12
6 Paper C    closed        20

    R 

    articles |>
  arrange(desc(citations))

    OUTPUT 

        title oa_status citations
1 Paper C    closed        20
2 Paper A      gold        12
3 Paper F     green         9
4 Paper D      gold         8
5 Paper B     green         5
6 Paper E    closed         3

    group_by() + summarise() is a pair you will use a lot. group_by() splits the data into groups, and summarise() then calculates one or more summary values per group:

    R 

    articles |>
  group_by(oa_status) |>
  summarise(average_citations = mean(citations))

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 3 × 2
  oa_status average_citations
  <chr>                 <dbl>
1 closed                 11.5
2 gold                   10
3 green                   7
    Challenge

    Challenge 5: Filter and select

    Your colleague from the repository team asks for the green OA articles. Using the articles data frame, keep only the articles with oa_status equal to "green", and show only their title and citations columns.

    R 

    articles |>
  filter(oa_status == "green") |>
  select(title, citations)

    OUTPUT 

        title citations
1 Paper B         5
2 Paper F         9
    Challenge

    Challenge 6: Group and summarise

    Your library director wants to know how many articles there are of each oa_status. Using the articles data frame, calculate this. (Hint: n() counts the rows in each group. Try summarise(count = n()).)

    R 

    articles |>
  group_by(oa_status) |>
  summarise(count = n())

    OUTPUT 

    # A tibble: 3 × 2
  oa_status count
  <chr>     <int>
1 closed        2
2 gold          2
3 green         2

    Key Points

    • Only ```{r} chunks are executed by Quarto, not ```r ones; chunks generate dashboard content
    • Objects are created with <-, functions are called as name(arguments), and vectors (c()) and data frames ($ accesses a column) store several values
    • Install packages once with install.packages() in the Console; load them in every session with library() inside the document
    • The pipe |> chains steps left to right instead of nesting functions
    • filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange() and group_by() + summarise() cover most day-to-day data wrangling

    Content from Building the Dashboard Skeleton

    Last updated on 2026-11-18 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do you turn a Quarto document into a dashboard?
    • How do you combine pages, rows and columns to lay out a dashboard?
    • How do you create value boxes and a card with an image?
    • How do you check that the structure works before adding real content?

    Objectives

    • Turn an existing Quarto document into a dashboard
    • Use Markdown headings to define pages, rows and columns
    • Create value boxes with placeholder values
    • Add a card with an image and text using Markdown
    • Render the dashboard and confirm its structure before adding actual content

    Why build a skeleton first?

    Before we add real-world data, we build a dashboard skeleton: a dashboard that already has its complete structure (two pages, rows, columns, value boxes and cards) but only placeholder content. This has two advantages. You can focus entirely on getting the layout right, without debugging data or code at the same time. And once the skeleton renders correctly, later episodes can focus on creating the content.

    The finished skeleton will have the following elements:

    Page Row Content
    Overview Row 1 three value boxes: Total Publications, Open Access Publications, Open Access Share
    Overview Row 2 left column: a chart card; right column: a card with an image and text
    Publications Row 1 a card for a table

    Turning your document into a dashboard

    You already have a Quarto document from the previous episode. A dashboard is the same kind of file with a different output format, so we keep the file and only change what it produces.

    1. Open your Quarto document in RStudio (if it is not open yet, double-click it in the Files pane)
    2. In the YAML header, change format: html to format: dashboard
    3. Click Render and look at the result

    Quarto now shows the same example text and the output of the code chunks as cards in a dashboard layout. A dashboard is built from cards, and each piece of content ends up in one of them. To build our OA monitoring dashboard, we start with an empty document. Delete all content below the YAML header.

    Your file should now look like this:

    YAML 

    ---
title: "Open Access Monitoring Dashboard"
format: dashboard
---

    Pages

    A level 1 heading creates a page, shown as a tab in the navigation bar. We create our first page called “Overview” below the YAML header:

    MARKDOWN 

    # Overview

    Rows

    Within a page, level 2 headings create rows. Add one, and control how much vertical space it takes with the height attribute in curly brackets:

    MARKDOWN 

    # Overview

## Row {height="20%"}

    The word “Row” is a label for humans reading the source; Quarto does not print it. What creates a row is the heading level (##) together with the dashboard’s orientation. You could write ## Anything and get the same result, but writing “Row” or “Column” makes the file easier to read. height only matters relative to other rows on the same page, so it will start to have a visible effect once we add a second row.

    Callout

    An empty row shows nothing

    A row without content is not displayed. If you render now, you will not see any change. Rows only appear once you put something inside them.

    Value boxes

    We want to fill our first row with three value boxes. A value box is a code chunk with the chunk option #| content: valuebox. Chunk options are special comment lines starting with #| at the very top of a chunk. Each sets one key: value pair. Here, title, icon and color style the box:

    MARKDOWN 

    # Overview

## Row {height="20%"}

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Total Publications"
#| icon: book
#| color: primary
"1,234"
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Open Access Publications"
#| icon: unlock
#| color: success
"765"
```

```{r}
#| content: valuebox
#| title: "Open Access Share"
#| icon: percent
#| color: warning
"62%"
```

    The last line of each chunk is the value that the box displays. For now, these are placeholder texts in quotation marks; in a later episode we replace them with calculated values.

    Click Render. You should see three value boxes on the “Overview” page.

    Callout

    Icons and colours

    The icon option accepts any name from the Bootstrap Icons library. Browse it, find an icon that fits and use its name, for example icon: unlock. The color option accepts a set of colour names (primary, success, warning, …) that we meet again in the styling episode. For all value box options, see Dashboard Data Display in the Quarto documentation.

    Columns and cards

    A level 3 heading (###) nested below a level 2 heading splits that row into columns. Add a second row with two columns. The left column gets a placeholder for our chart. Remember: every code chunk’s output automatically becomes its own card, and a chunk option title gives the card a title:

    MARKDOWN 

    ## Row {height="80%"}

### Column {width="65%"}

```{r}
#| title: "Open Access Share by Publication Year"
"The chart will go here."
```

    The width attribute works for columns like height does for rows. When you click Render you should see a wide card with your placeholder text below the value boxes.

    A card with an image and text

    Cards are not limited to code output. A card that contains Markdown is created with a .card div: a block that starts and ends with three colons. You have already learned the image syntax in the Markdown episode. Add the right column with an image of the Open Access logo, including alt text:

    MARKDOWN 

    ### Column {width="35%"}

::: {.card title="About Open Access"}

![Open Access logo, an open padlock](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:FilePath/Open_Access_logo_PLoS_transparent.svg)

:::

    Render again. The page now has two rows, and the second row has two columns side by side.

    A second page

    Now we want to add our second page “Publications” with one placeholder card for the table we build later:

    MARKDOWN 

    # Publications

## Row

```{r}
#| title: "Publications by Publisher"
"The table will go here."
```

    After rendering, check that the navigation bar shows two page tabs, “Overview” and “Publications”. The skeleton now contains every component we want in our dashboard.

    Callout

    What about making it look good?

    We have not touched colours, fonts or themes. Everything you see is default Quarto styling. That is deliberate: a later episode is dedicated to styling. For now, the goal is a correct structure.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: A text card about OA routes

    Your dashboard should explain the most common routes to open access, so that colleagues who are new to the topic can understand the numbers. Add a card below the ‘About Open Access’ card in the right column of your Overview page that has:

    • the title “OA publishing routes”
    • a list of three routes, each with its name in bold:
      • Gold: published open access in an OA journal
      • Green: a copy is deposited in a repository
      • Hybrid: open access article in a subscription journal
    • a link to the Directory of Open Access Journals with a short sentence such as “Find open access journals and articles”

    Render your dashboard and check that all three elements appear.

    A text card is a ::: block with the class .card. The title is set in curly braces: ::: {.card title="..."}. Inside the card, you write plain Markdown. Remember, a list needs an empty line before it and a space after each -.

    MARKDOWN 

    ::: {.card title="OA publishing routes"}

- **Gold**: published open access in an OA journal
- **Green**: a copy is deposited in a repository
- **Hybrid**: open access article in a subscription journal

Find open access journals and articles: [Directory of Open Access Journals](https://doaj.org)
:::
    Challenge

    Challenge 2: Orientation experiment

    Your university manager would prefer the layout rotated: the three OA indicators stacked in a column on the left. Without touching any headings, change the YAML header so that level 2 headings create columns instead of rows. Render and describe what changed. Then change it back.

    Remember the orientation setting from the “Introduction to Quarto Dashboards” episode, and how it is nested in the YAML header.

    YAML 

    ---
title: "Open Access Monitoring Dashboard"
format:
  dashboard:
    orientation: columns
---

    Level 2 headings now create columns instead of rows, and the height attribute of the “rows” no longer makes sense (you would use width now). Level 3 headings inside a column now create rows. Revert the change to continue with the lesson.

    Key Points

    • Create a dashboard by setting format: dashboard in the YAML header
    • # creates a page, ## a row, ### a column; height and width set their relative size
    • Value boxes are chunks with #| content: valuebox
    • Every chunk’s output becomes a card; Markdown text and images go into .card divs
